claims.text: Today an sgit vault is protected by one symmetric read key and a write key that only the server checks.
claims.quote: Today an sgit vault is protected by one symmetric read key and a write key that only the server checks

claims.text: Because the read key is symmetric, whoever can read can also produce data every client accepts, so a read-key holder who can write to the store can author history.
claims.quote: An sgit vault's read key is symmetric, so whoever can read can also produce data every client accepts.

claims.text: From the passphrase, PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations derives the read key and the write key.
claims.quote: From the passphrase, PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations derives two keys.

claims.text: Every stored object is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so a client can check the server returned exactly what was stored, with no key and no trust.
claims.quote: Every stored object is named by the hash of its ciphertext, so a client can check that the server returned exactly what was stored, with no key and no trust.

claims.text: Commits are signed with ECDSA P-256 by the key of the clone that made them.
claims.quote: Commits are also signed, with ECDSA P-256, by the key of the clone that made them.

claims.text: Commit signatures do not close the gap, because a signing key is trusted when its file decrypts under the read key, and a read-key holder can make such a file.
claims.quote: Commit signatures do not save the day, because a signing key is trusted when its file decrypts under the read key, and a read-key holder can make such a file.

claims.text: sgit's threat model lists the forgery as a by-design risk and carries a test that performs it and asserts it still succeeds, so the gap cannot be quietly forgotten.
claims.quote: It carries a test that performs the forgery against an in-memory host and asserts that it still succeeds, so the gap cannot be quietly forgotten

claims.text: Making the read key public and the write key private fails, because whatever decrypts must be secret and the public half can always be derived from the private half.
claims.quote: fails, because whatever decrypts must be secret, and the public half can always be derived from the private half.

claims.text: Both designs share a first step: a vault signing key, an Ed25519 key derived from the passphrase along a third path, with writers signing branch pointers and the index.
claims.quote: today's vaults can get a vault signing key: an Ed25519 key derived from the passphrase along a third path

claims.text: Ed25519 is chosen because its signatures are deterministic, so the browser and the command line can share byte-for-byte test vectors.
claims.quote: Ed25519 is chosen because its signatures are deterministic, so the browser and the command line can share byte-for-byte test vectors.

claims.text: The writer signature is estimated at one and a half to two weeks for the command line, with the same work in the web UI.
claims.quote: The analysis estimates one and a half to two weeks for the command line, with the same work in the web UI.

value.unit: weeks for the command line, upper estimate

claims.text: Design 1, native PKI vault mode: two key pairs, neither derivable from the other, X25519 for reading and Ed25519 for writing, so a reader cannot write and a host cannot forge.
claims.quote: Two key pairs, neither derivable from the other: one for reading, one for writing.

claims.text: A random data key is sealed to the read public key rather than encrypting each object to it, because public-key encryption is randomised and sgit depends on deterministic tree encryption.
claims.quote: Public-key encryption is randomised: the same tree encrypted twice gives different bytes.

claims.text: The object store, content addressing, trees, sync, merge, partial clones and the command line do not change; only key creation, how the data key reaches a reader, and what authorises a write.
claims.quote: What does not change: the object store, content addressing, trees, sync, merge, partial clones and the command line.

claims.text: The write-only depositor is the capability today's design cannot express: it can encrypt but not read, so write-only means append to its own inbox branch.
claims.quote: A depositor can encrypt but not read, so it cannot read the current tree to change it: write-only means append.

claims.text: A self-certifying vault id means a new write key is a new vault; the cleaner design derives the id from an owner root key that signs a writer set.
claims.quote: A self-certifying vault id means a new write key is a new vault.

claims.text: The algorithms, Ed25519, X25519, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM, are all available in the Python cryptography library and in current browsers' Web Crypto.
claims.quote: Ed25519, X25519, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM, all available in the Python cryptography library and in current browsers' Web Crypto.

claims.text: Design 2, sealed files: an inner envelope sealed to named people's public keys inside the vault's own encryption, on either vault mode, with the private key anywhere.
claims.quote: An inner envelope, sealed to named people's public keys, inside the vault's own encryption.

claims.text: Any vault writer can replace a sealed file without being able to read it, because sealing needs only public keys; signed envelopes and per-path author rules answer that.
claims.quote: any vault writer can replace a sealed file without being able to read it, because sealing needs only public keys.

claims.text: The proposed format is age v1: specified, small and audited, openable with the stock age tool, with a plugin protocol for keys that live elsewhere.
claims.quote: It is specified, small and audited; a sealed file can be opened with the stock age tool without sgit

claims.text: age's payload cipher, ChaCha20-Poly1305, is not in Web Crypto, so the browser would use the reference TypeScript implementation.
claims.quote: age's payload cipher, ChaCha20-Poly1305, is not in Web Crypto, so the browser would use the reference TypeScript implementation.

claims.text: Thirty services and tools were checked on 9 October 2026, from their own documentation, as places a private key could live.
claims.quote: we checked thirty services and tools on 9 October 2026, from their own documentation.

claims.text: The format the remote key services share is RSA-OAEP-256, not X25519, so sealed files would also need an rsa-oaep-256 recipient type.
claims.quote: The format the remote services share is RSA-OAEP-256, not X25519.

claims.text: The three large cloud key services do not offer X25519 decryption; AWS offers key agreement on NIST curves only and Google uses X25519 only inside X-Wing.
claims.quote: The three large cloud key services do not offer X25519 decryption

claims.text: Approval of each decryption by a person is rare: Fortanix's quorum policy and Vault's control groups provide it; cloud key services give logs and access rules, not a step that asks someone.
claims.quote: Approval of each decryption by a person is rare. Fortanix's quorum policy and Vault's control groups provide it

claims.text: No age plugin backed by a cloud key service was found, although age's plugin design names cloud key services as a purpose.
claims.quote: We found no age plugin backed by a cloud key service

claims.text: Sealed files do not hide file names, paths, sizes or history from vault members, a removed recipient keeps what was sealed to them, and it is only as strong as the provider.
claims.quote: It does not hide file names, paths, sizes or history from vault members; a recipient removed later keeps what was sealed to them before

claims.text: Limits stay in both designs: a host can still withhold data or serve an older signed state, and a reader you remove keeps what they already read.
claims.quote: a host can still withhold data or serve an older signed state; a reader you remove keeps what they already read

claims.text: Nothing described is implemented; there is no code and no release date, and the effort figures are the designers' estimates.
claims.quote: Nothing described here is implemented. Effort figures are the designers' estimates.

claims.text: None of this is new: Tahoe-LAFS separates read and write capabilities, Hypercore and Dat use a key pair as a feed's identity, git-crypt and SOPS seal files, age puts decryption where the key lives.
claims.quote: Tahoe-LAFS separates read and write capabilities for mutable files in nearly this shape.

claims.text: Is there a simpler construction than two key pairs that gives readers no write power and writers no derivable read power, and still works in browsers?
claims.quote: Is there a simpler construction that gives readers no write power and writers no derivable read power, and still works in browsers?

claims.text: Should sealed files use age v1 or a custom HPKE envelope that stays pure Web Crypto and gives up the ecosystem?
claims.quote: age v1 or a custom HPKE envelope?

claims.text: Is a transparency log or a witness worth the complexity, given a host can still serve an old signed state to someone who never saw a newer one?
claims.quote: Is a transparency log or a witness worth the complexity?

claims.text: Is running two vault modes side by side worth the extra surface, or should the PKI mode eventually replace the symmetric one?
claims.quote: Is the extra surface worth it, or should the PKI mode eventually replace the symmetric one?

claims.text: The same envelope can carry a vault capability to a person: sgit share --to dinis would seal it to Dinis's published key, so no passphrase passes through chat or shell history.
claims.quote: sgit share --to dinis would seal it to Dinis's published key, so no passphrase passes through chat, the command line or shell history.
